steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on COFT-AD, a contrastive fine-tuning method for few-shot anomaly detection. It should motivate the few-shot setting, discuss what is wrong with existing few-shot methods, explain our idea and its loss components, and finish with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Anomaly detection and why normal training data can be scarce
2. Few-shot anomaly detection (FSAD) and limits of existing methods
3. Our approach: transfer learning from pre-trained weights, and two problems with reusing them directly
4. COFT-AD: three loss components
5. Evaluation and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Anomaly detection (AD)
- fundamental ML problem; applications: defect identification, surveillance, autonomous driving
- usual assumption: normal images abundant, labeled anomalies non-exhaustive -> train on normal images only (one-class classification)
- not always true: system must work instantly on new task with limited data; normal samples expensive / time-consuming to get
- especially at initial stages of bootstrapping an AD system

2. FSAD
- only a few normal, no abnormal images; growing interest
- Sheynin et al.: generative adversarial model, transformed vs generated patches; adversarial models tricky to tune; multiple transformations at test time -> computation overhead
- RegAD: common model over multiple classes, feature registration proxy task; needs normal images from multiple known classes (restrictive)
- GraphCore (from PatchCore): compare test patches to few-shot training patches
- RegAD + GraphCore: assume anomalies = local appearance variations; only shown on highly constrained industrial tasks
- summary: tricky hyper-parameter tuning or overly restrictive assumptions on anomaly presentation

3. Our approach
- goal: FSAD for wide variety of data domains, no complicated hyper-parameter tuning
- combine transfer learning from pre-trained model + representation learning on few-shot normal data
- pre-trained backbone on large source dataset (e.g. ImageNet): powerful low-level feature extractors, better initialization
- particularly useful in few-shot: not enough data to learn from scratch
- but direct reuse may not use limited supervision well, two factors:
  - AD needs features separating normal from abnormal; pre-training optimized for different task (semantic classification of ImageNet)
  - covariate shift: source domain (pre-training) vs target domain (where anomalies detected)

4. COFT-AD (unsupervised fine-tuning)
- customized loss with three components, to ameliorate covariate shift
- (a) contrastive loss on all few-shot normal examples: sample close to its augmented versions -> adapt to target distribution, robust to natural variations
- (b) cross-instance positive pair loss: two randomly sampled normal images close -> tight cluster, helps density based inference; differs from standard contrastive training
- (c) if prior knowledge on anomalies: synthesized negative examples, negative pair loss -> better separation
- empirical finding: how negatives are synthesised has high impact on FSAD performance; use carefully
- overview in Fig. 1

5. Evaluation / contributions
- controlled setups (data designed to have certain properties) + real-world FSAD
- handles greater diversity of domains, strong performance
- contributions: transfer learning view + contrastive fine-tuning; cross-instance positive pair loss; negative pair loss with synthesized negatives; 3 controlled datasets + 4 real-world industrial defect datasets, very competitive

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Anomaly detection (AD), i.e. identifying anomalous data, is a fundamental problem in machine learning and it has a lot of potential in different applications, for example defect identification, surveillance and autonomous driving. Usually it is assumed that there are plenty of normal images, while the labeled anomaly examples are not exhaustive. So anomaly detection models are trained with normal images only, which is also called one-class classification. But this is not always the case. Some practical applications need the AD system to work right away when it is deployed on a new task where only limited data exists, or getting normal samples is expensive or takes a lot of time. So we may not have large numbers of normal images to build a good anomaly detection model, especially at the start when the AD system is being bootstrapped.

Few-shot anomaly detection (FSAD), where there are only a few normal images and no abnormal ones, has emerged as a solution for building an anomaly detection system when normal training examples are lacking, and the community is getting more interested in this topic. There are only a few pioneering works. Sheynin et al. developed a generative adversarial model that distinguishes transformed image patches from generated ones. But adversarial models like this can be tricky to tune, and they also need multiple transformations on the test samples at inference time, which adds computation overhead. RegAD is more recent and learns a common model over multiple classes of normal images with a feature registration proxy task. However it needs a training set with normal images from multiple known classes, and this is a more restrictive setting. GraphCore comes from PatchCore and approaches FSAD by comparing test patches to the few-shot training ones. Both RegAD and GraphCore assume that anomalies are caused by variations in local appearance, and they only show success on highly constrained industrial anomaly detection tasks. So the existing FSAD methods either make training complicated with tricky hyper-parameter tuning or make overly restrictive assumptions about how anomalies are presented, and this limits how they can be applied to a wider range of tasks.

In this work we want to develop a few-shot anomaly detection framework that works for a wide variety of data domains and does not need complicated hyper-parameter tuning. To do this we combine transfer learning from a pre-trained model with representation learning on the few-shot normal data that we have. If we re-use weights of a backbone network that was pre-trained on a large source domain dataset, e.g. ImageNet, we can exploit powerful low-level feature extractors and get a better initialization of the network parameters for downstream tasks. We think re-using pre-trained weights could especially help few-shot anomaly detection, because there is not enough training data to learn good representations from scratch. But existing works point out that directly reusing the pre-trained weights may not make full use of the limited supervision in the downstream task, and there are two reasons for this. The first reason is that anomaly detection needs a feature representation that separates normal samples from abnormal ones, but the representations learned in pre-training were optimized for a different task, like semantic image classification on ImageNet, so they are not necessarily optimal for anomaly detection downstream. The second reason is covariate shift, which can hurt performance. Covariate shift comes from the difference in distribution between the source domain data that was used for pre-training the model and the target domain data where the anomalies are to be detected.

- COFT-AD: unsupervised fine-tuning to adapt pre-trained weights; customized loss with three components to ameliorate covariate shift
- (a) contrastive loss on all few-shot normal examples: sample close to its augmented versions -> adapt to target distribution, robust to natural variations
- (b) cross-instance positive pair loss: two randomly sampled normal images close -> tight cluster for density based inference; not the same as standard contrastive training
- (c) with prior knowledge on anomalies: synthesized negative examples + negative pair loss -> better separation; how negatives are synthesised matters a lot
- overview in Fig. 1

- evaluation: controlled setups + real-world FSAD; handles diverse domains with strong performance
- contributions list (4 bullets): transfer learning view; cross-instance positive pair loss; negative pair loss; results on 3 controlled + 4 real-world industrial defect datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Anomaly detection (AD), i.e. identifying anomalous data, is a fundamental problem in machine learning and it has a lot of potential in different applications, for example defect identification, surveillance and autonomous driving. Usually it is assumed that there are plenty of normal images, while the labeled anomaly examples are not exhaustive. So anomaly detection models are trained with normal images only, which is also called one-class classification. But this is not always the case. Some practical applications need the AD system to work right away when it is deployed on a new task where only limited data exists, or getting normal samples is expensive or takes a lot of time. So we may not have large numbers of normal images to build a good anomaly detection model, especially at the start when the AD system is being bootstrapped.

Few-shot anomaly detection (FSAD), where there are only a few normal images and no abnormal ones, has emerged as a solution for building an anomaly detection system when normal training examples are lacking, and the community is getting more interested in this topic. There are only a few pioneering works. Sheynin et al. developed a generative adversarial model that distinguishes transformed image patches from generated ones. But adversarial models like this can be tricky to tune, and they also need multiple transformations on the test samples at inference time, which adds computation overhead. RegAD is more recent and learns a common model over multiple classes of normal images with a feature registration proxy task. However it needs a training set with normal images from multiple known classes, and this is a more restrictive setting. GraphCore comes from PatchCore and approaches FSAD by comparing test patches to the few-shot training ones. Both RegAD and GraphCore assume that anomalies are caused by variations in local appearance, and they only show success on highly constrained industrial anomaly detection tasks. So the existing FSAD methods either make training complicated with tricky hyper-parameter tuning or make overly restrictive assumptions about how anomalies are presented, and this limits how they can be applied to a wider range of tasks.

In this work we want to develop a few-shot anomaly detection framework that works for a wide variety of data domains and does not need complicated hyper-parameter tuning. To do this we combine transfer learning from a pre-trained model with representation learning on the few-shot normal data that we have. If we re-use weights of a backbone network that was pre-trained on a large source domain dataset, e.g. ImageNet, we can exploit powerful low-level feature extractors and get a better initialization of the network parameters for downstream tasks. We think re-using pre-trained weights could especially help few-shot anomaly detection, because there is not enough training data to learn good representations from scratch. But existing works point out that directly reusing the pre-trained weights may not make full use of the limited supervision in the downstream task, and there are two reasons for this. The first reason is that anomaly detection needs a feature representation that separates normal samples from abnormal ones, but the representations learned in pre-training were optimized for a different task, like semantic image classification on ImageNet, so they are not necessarily optimal for anomaly detection downstream. The second reason is covariate shift, which can hurt performance. Covariate shift comes from the difference in distribution between the source domain data that was used for pre-training the model and the target domain data where the anomalies are to be detected.

To deal with these challenges we propose an unsupervised fine-tuning approach called “COntrastive Fine-Tuning for few-shot Anomaly Detection” (COFT-AD), which adapts the pre-trained weights to the downstream few-shot anomaly detection task. To reduce the covariate shift between source and target domain data, we design customized loss functions that have three components. Each component encourages a desirable property in the learnt representation space when it is adapted to the anomaly detection task in the target domain. The first component is a contrastive loss that is defined on all the few-shot normal examples available. Optimizing a contrastive loss helps adapt the pre-trained model weights to the distribution of the downstream anomaly detection dataset. It does this by encouraging one sample and its augmented versions to be close in the feature space. This makes the model more robust to natural variations within the normal data. The second component optimizes the representations further for the anomaly detection task, by encouraging the normal samples to form a tight cluster in the feature space so that density based anomaly inference is made easier. For this we use a cross-instance positive pair loss that encourages the feature embeddings of two randomly sampled normal images to be close. This is different from standard contrastive training, because closeness is encouraged between two different normal samples and not between a sample and its augmented version. Finally, if we have prior knowledge on the anomalies, we can synthesize negative examples that simulate anomalies and use them in an additional negative pair loss, and this loss encourages better separation between the normal samples and their negative pairs. In our analysis we find empirically that the method used to synthesise negative samples has high impact on FSAD performance, so it should be used carefully and with prior knowledge on the nature of the anomalies. An overall illustration of the proposed framework is shown in Fig. 1.

We evaluate COFT-AD extensively on a diverse range of anomaly detection tasks. These cover controlled setups, where normal and anomalous data are deliberately designed to show certain properties, and also real-world data FSAD, where we have no control over the nature of the anomalies. The evaluations show that our method is able to handle more diversity in data domains and still keep strong performance. Our contributions are as follows:

- We approach few-shot anomaly detection that is hyper-parameter friendly and versatile in data domain from a transfer learning perspective. We use contrastive fine-tuning on few-shot normal samples in the target domain to adapt the pre-trained model weights to the target domain distribution.

- We also introduce a cross-instance positive pair loss so that normal samples form a tight cluster in the embedding space, which is better for density-based anomaly detection.

- When prior knowledge on how anomalies are presented is available, we also add a negative pair loss with synthesized negative samples to get better separation between normal and abnormal samples.

- We show the effectiveness of the proposed method, COntrastive Fine-Tuning for few-shot Anomaly Detection (COFT-AD), on 3 controlled anomaly detection datasets and 4 real-world industrial defect identification datasets, where it achieves very competitive performance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Identifying anomalous data, a.k.a. anomaly detection (AD), is a fundamental problem in machine learning research with significant potential in various applications, such as defect identification [1], surveillance [2], and autonomous driving [3]. It is typically assumed that normal images are abundant, while labeled anomaly examples are non-exhaustive. Hence, anomaly detection models are trained only with normal images, also known as one-class classification. However, this is not always the case. For example, some practical applications require an AD system to function instantly when deployed on a new task with limited existing data, or when acquiring normal samples is expensive or time-consuming. As a result, large numbers of normal images may not be available for building a good anomaly detection model, especially in the initial stages of bootstrapping an AD system.

In response to the need for building an anomaly detection system with insufficient normal training examples, few-shot anomaly detection (FSAD), where only a few normal and no abnormal images are available, has emerged as a solution [4,5,6], and the community is showing growing interest in this topic. Among the limited pioneering works, Sheynin et al. [4] developed a generative adversarial model to distinguish transformed image patches from generated ones. However, such adversarial models can be tricky to tune [7] and require multiple transformations on test samples at inference time, which results in additional computation overhead. The more recent RegAD [5] learns a common model over multiple classes of normal images using a feature registration proxy task, but it requires a training set with normal images from multiple known classes, which is a more restrictive setting. GraphCore [6], which stems from PatchCore [8], approached FSAD by comparing test patches to few-shot training ones. However, both RegAD and GraphCore assume that anomalies are caused by variations in local appearance, and their success has only been demonstrated on highly constrained industrial anomaly detection tasks. In summary, existing FSAD methods either complicate training with tricky hyper-parameter tuning [4] or make overly restrictive assumptions on the presentation of anomalies [8,6], which limits their applicability to a wider range of tasks.

In this work, we aim to develop a few-shot anomaly detection framework that is applicable to a wide variety of data domains without complicated hyper-parameter tuning. We achieve this by combining transfer learning from a pre-trained model with representation learning on the available few-shot normal data. Re-using weights from a backbone network pre-trained on a large source domain dataset, e.g. ImageNet [9], allows us to exploit powerful, low-level feature extractors and a better initialization of network parameters [10] for downstream tasks. We believe that re-using pre-trained weights could particularly benefit few-shot anomaly detection, since the training data is insufficient for learning good representations from scratch. However, as highlighted in existing works [11,12], directly reusing the pre-trained weights may not fully utilize the limited supervision in the downstream task, because of two factors. First, the anomaly detection task requires a feature representation that separates normal samples from abnormal ones. The representations learned during pre-training are optimized for a different task, such as semantic image classification of ImageNet, and are therefore not necessarily optimal for downstream anomaly detection. Second, performance can be hindered by covariate shift [13], which results from the difference in distribution between the source domain data (used for pre-training the model) and the target domain data (in which anomalies are to be detected).

To tackle these challenges, we propose an unsupervised fine-tuning approach, named “COntrastive Fine-Tuning for few-shot Anomaly Detection” (COFT-AD), which adapts pre-trained weights to the downstream few-shot anomaly detection task. To ameliorate the covariate shift between source and target domain data, we first design customized loss functions with three components, each of which encourages a desirable property in the learnt representation space when adapted towards the anomaly detection task in the target domain. The first component is a contrastive loss [14], defined on all available few-shot normal examples. Optimizing a contrastive loss helps adapt pre-trained model weights to the distribution of the downstream anomaly detection dataset. Specifically, this is achieved by encouraging closeness between a sample and its augmented versions in the feature space, which improves the model’s robustness to natural variations within the normal data. The second component further optimizes representations for the anomaly detection task by encouraging normal samples to form a tight cluster in the feature space, so that a density based anomaly inference is facilitated. We achieve this with a cross-instance positive pair loss that encourages closeness between the feature embeddings of two randomly sampled normal images. Note that this differs from standard contrastive training, since closeness is encouraged between two different normal samples rather than between a sample and its augmented version. Finally, when prior knowledge on the anomalies is available, we can synthesize negative examples [15] to simulate anomalies in an additional negative pair loss, which encourages better separation between the normal samples and their negative pairs. Our analysis empirically reveals that the method by which negative samples are synthesised has a high impact on FSAD performance, and that it should be used carefully, with prior knowledge on the nature of anomalies. We extensively evaluate COFT-AD on a diverse range of anomaly detection tasks, covering both controlled setups, in which normal and anomalous data are deliberately designed to exhibit certain properties, and real-world data FSAD, where the nature of anomalies is out of our control. The extensive evaluations demonstrate that our method can handle greater diversity in data domains while maintaining strong performance. We summarize our contributions as follows:

- We approach hyper-parameter friendly and data domain versatile few-shot anomaly detection from a transfer learning perspective, adopting contrastive fine-tuning on few-shot normal samples in the target domain to adapt pre-trained model weights to the target domain distribution.

- We further introduce a cross-instance positive pair loss that encourages normal samples to form a tight cluster in the embedding space for better density-based anomaly detection.

- In scenarios where prior knowledge on anomaly presentations is available, we further incorporate a negative pair loss with synthesized negative samples to encourage better separation between normal and abnormal samples.

- We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, COntrastive Fine-Tuning for few-shot Anomaly Detection (COFT-AD), on 3 controlled anomaly detection datasets and 4 real-world industrial defect identification datasets, where it achieves very competitive performance.
